---
title: Model presets
description: "The bundled xs to xl size ladder, which node owns each setting, overrides, and application presets."
engine: markdown
---

`rf.Model.xs(...)`, `.sm(...)`, `.md(...)`, `.lg(...)`, and `.xl(...)` build the
same schema with different architecture defaults. Start with `xs` or `sm` to
establish a working payment model, then compare larger configurations on
validation data. See [Your first model](../learn/your-first-model.qmd) for the basic
training workflow.

Each factory call builds fresh model state. To reuse a trained model, load its
[saved artifact](../guides/checkpoints-ema-and-resuming.qmd), then adapt it through
another fit or [schema evolution](../guides/schema-mutation.qmd) as the task needs.

## Bundled sizes

These are the bundled revision-1 configurations:

| Setting | `xs` | `sm` | `md` | `lg` | `xl` |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Shared width, `d_model` | 64 | 128 | 256 | 384 | 512 |
| Root encoder layers | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 6 |
| Child branch encoder layers | 1 | 1 | 2 | 2 | 3 |
| Root, branch, and leaf heads | 2 | 4 | 8 | 8 | 8 |
| Root attention outputs | 1 | 2 | 4 | 8 | 16 |
| Child branch attention outputs | 1 | 2 | 4 | 4 | 8 |
| Feed-forward multiplier, `ffnx` | 8 | 8 | 8 | 8 | 8 |

Every size uses MHA encoders and zero dropout. Each attention reduction has one
layer and positional information; its heads and dropout inherit the owning
branch. Leaf decoders use query pooling, one cross-attention block
(`n_linear=1`), and automatic decoder positioning (`decoder_position=None`).
Automatic positioning is off for a single predicted position and on when the
target has more than one position.

RelFlow's hidden activations use tanh GELU, and its neural normalization uses
RMSNorm with epsilon `1e-5`. These choices are fixed. Pretrained text encoders
retain their own architectures.

A size name describes defaults, rather than a parameter-count range or a
prediction-quality guarantee. The schema, vocabularies, requested decoders,
and external text encoders also determine model size.

## Which node owns a setting?

A preset fills three separate scopes:

| Scope | Settings supplied |
| --- | --- |
| Model root | Encoder `n_layers`, `n_heads`, `ffnx`, `attention`, `dropout`, and root `reduction`. |
| Every child branch | Its own encoder settings and `reduction`, at every nesting depth. |
| Each leaf | Decoder `n_heads`, `ffnx`, `pooling`, `n_linear`, `dropout`, and `decoder_position`. |

`d_model` is shared across the whole model. Root overrides apply to the root;
branch overrides apply to that branch. Leaf decoder heads do not inherit a
containing branch's override.

For example, take the sequence schema from
[Add transaction history](../learn/add-transaction-history.qmd), with a hidden
dispute target on every retained transaction. This `sm` model changes root
depth, the history's feed-forward multiplier, and the dispute decoder's heads
independently:

```python
import relflow as rf

model = rf.Model.sm(
    n_layers=3,
    trxns=rf.Branch(
        length=32,
        overflow="tail",
        ffnx=4,
        booked_at=rf.DateParts(
            dateparts=["day_of_month", "day_of_week", "hour_of_day"],
        ),
        amount=rf.Number,
        merchant=rf.Category,
        disputed=rf.Boolean(mask=True, n_heads=2),
    ),
)
```

The history keeps the `sm` branch depth of one layer. Its leaves keep their
own `ffnx=8` defaults. Changing the history's multiplier does not change them.
Each `ffnx` must be a positive integer; its hidden feed-forward width is
`ffnx * d_model`.

```{typst}
//| label: fig-preset-ownership
//| fig-cap: "The payment root, transaction branch, and field decoders have separate settings. Their ownership follows the schema."
//| fig-alt: "A payment root contains one repeated trxns branch with booked_at DateParts, amount Number, merchant Category, and a hidden disputed Boolean target for every transaction. Root and branch own separate contexts; the nested dispute target owns its decoder."
#tree(node("payment", kind: "root", detail: "Root context", children: (

    node("amount", type: "Number"),
    node("merchant", type: "Category"),
    node("disputed", kind: "target", type: "Boolean", detail: "Every transaction; own decoder"),
  )),
)))
```

The multiplier controls a branch's sequence encoder, coordinate encoder, and
learned reduction. On a leaf it controls query-decoder feed-forward blocks and
aligned sibling-context projection. It does not change the number of retained
transactions or the shared output width.

## Overrides and explicit None

Resolution follows this order at each node:

1. An explicitly supplied option wins, including one equal to the ordinary default.
2. An omitted option uses that scope's preset value.
3. Options outside the preset keep their ordinary datatype or branch defaults.

An explicit reduction replaces the whole reduction object. For example,
`reduction=rf.Attention()` selects one output and one layer even under `xl`.
It does not inherit `xl`'s output count. `rf.Mean()` and `None` also replace the
preset reduction completely.

`None` is a deliberate value where the option accepts it:

| Option | Meaning of `None` |
| --- | --- |
| Root or branch `attention` | Disable encoder attention; the reduction remains separately configured. |
| Root or branch `reduction` | Pass through routed child slots instead of reducing them. |
| Node `dropout` | Use zero dropout. |
| Leaf `decoder_position` | Use the automatic scalar/repeated-target policy. |
| Attention reduction `n_heads` or `dropout` | Inherit the owning branch's value. |

A width override must be compatible with every effective attention head count.
It does not rewrite branch or leaf heads. Invalid geometry is rejected at the
affected address. Reusing a branch or leaf definition in another model creates
a separately resolved tree and leaves the original definition unchanged.

The preset leaves history lengths, overflow, field roles, queries, objective
weights, and datatype-specific options to the application. Set batch size on
the loop, such as `model.fit(data, batch_size=128, max_epochs=30)`. Constructor
batch size remains the initial value, defaulting to one. Optimization,
schedulers, training budgets, hardware, and data-loader settings belong to the
[training workflow](../guides/training-options.qmd), not the size profile.

For YAML configurations, `preset: sm` chooses the same bundled policy.
Python overrides win over file options, which win over the preset. See
[Model templates](../guides/model-templates.qmd).

## Save, load, and extend

The resolved schema records the model's actual architecture. `model.preset`
holds the immutable construction policy, including its name and revision.
Saving preserves both. Loading uses those saved values rather than applying a
newer version of a bundled preset.

```python
model.save("artifacts/payment-history.rf")
restored = rf.Model.load("artifacts/payment-history.rf")
restored.extend(
    rf.where("address") == rf.Address(),
    country=rf.Category,
)
```

The new `country` field receives the saved `sm` leaf defaults. Existing nodes
keep their resolved options, including the earlier dispute-head override.
Updating a trained model does not reapply the preset to its existing tree.
See [Schema mutation](../guides/schema-mutation.qmd) for learned-state boundaries.

`rf.Model(schema=schema)` restores an already resolved architecture. It carries
no preset policy unless loaded from a saved artifact that contains one; newly
extended nodes then use ordinary defaults. Preset factories reject `schema=`
because the schema already specifies its architecture.

Selecting another size constructs a new architecture. Increasing width, depth,
or output count on a trained model does not provide automatic weight
compatibility.

## Define an application preset

Use `rf.presets.Preset` with frozen root, branch, and leaf configurations, then
bind it to a model subclass with `rf.presets.factory`:

```python
compact = rf.presets.Preset(
    name="payment-compact",
    revision=1,
    d_model=96,
    root=rf.presets.BranchDefaults(
        n_layers=2,
        n_heads=4,
        reduction=rf.Attention(n_outputs=2),
    ),
    branch=rf.presets.BranchDefaults(
        n_layers=1,
        n_heads=4,
        reduction=rf.Attention(n_outputs=1),
    ),
    leaf=rf.presets.LeafDefaults(n_heads=4),
)

class PaymentModel(rf.Model):
    compact = rf.presets.factory(compact)

payment_model = PaymentModel.compact(
    trxns=rf.Branch(
        length=32,
        overflow="tail",
        booked_at=rf.DateParts(
            dateparts=["day_of_month", "day_of_week", "hour_of_day"],
        ),
        amount=rf.Number,
        merchant=rf.Category,
        disputed=rf.Boolean(mask=True),
    ),
)
```

The result is a `PaymentModel`. Inherited built-in factories also construct the
calling subclass. Policy names must be nonempty and revisions positive; use a
new revision when changing an application's defaults. Common leaf settings also
apply to registered third-party tensorfields without replacing their extension
options.

Ordinary Python construction uses these factories rather than a `preset=` or
`size=` selector. A schema child named `preset` or `size` remains an ordinary
field. YAML templates reserve their own top-level `preset` entry.

## Capacity, embeddings, and cost

The size ladder increases shared width and root depth while keeping child
encoders shallower. More reduction outputs let a branch send more context to
its parent. These are useful axes to compare; their values are engineering
starting points rather than benchmark-derived quality thresholds.

Each branch owns separate weights, and each decoded field adds its own decoder.
Wider feed-forward layers, more branches, deeper encoders, longer histories,
and larger vocabularies can all increase memory or compute. Attention output
slots also add learned parameters and affect the parent's input size. Reducing
those slots occurs after that branch's encoder, so it does not remove the
branch's own input-attention work.


`n_layers` counts sequence encoder blocks. A branch with multiple active direct
leaves can also have a separate coordinate-attention block. Head count partitions
the shared width; adding heads at a fixed width does not multiply the MHA
projection parameter count.

An attention reduction may have more outputs than inputs. In that case it
expands context rather than compressing it. Mean reduction emits one summary;
no reduction preserves routed child slots. Completely inactive subtrees emit
no structural outputs. See [Branch](../datatypes/branch.qmd) for these contracts.

With root `embed=True`, the default `xs` model emits one width-64 vector, while
`md` emits four width-256 vectors. Set `reduction=rf.Attention(n_outputs=1)`
when an application needs one root vector, then evaluate the resulting
bottleneck. Reduction outputs are context vectors, not additional prediction
records; target coordinates still come from the schema.

Zero dropout permits the eligible packed encoder training path for partially
present inputs. Nonzero dropout can change both learning and execution cost.
GQA, MQA, Mean reduction, and disabled attention likewise change model behavior;
measure them on the actual task. GQA and MQA apply to branch encoders; reduction
and decoder query attention retain MHA. Turning off reduction positioning alone does
not make a branch with positional encoder attention permutation invariant.

Compare task quality on fixed validation splits and record the actual parameter
count, peak memory, and throughput for the schema and hardware used. Increase
one capacity axis at a time. A larger preset can underfit, overfit, or cost more
without improving the task. See [Evaluation](../learn/evaluation.qmd) and
[Performance](../guides/performance.qmd).
